lesson.title: The Price Tag on Every Chemical Bond
lesson.summary: Bond enthalpy is the average energy needed to break one mole of a particular type of bond in the gas phase, and it is always a positive quantity because breaking a bond always costs energy.
lesson.body:
Bond energy, in general terms, is the strength of attraction holding two atoms together. Bond enthalpy sharpens that idea into a specific thermochemical quantity: it is the enthalpy change, measured at constant pressure, for breaking one mole of a given type of bond between two gas-phase atoms, so that both fragments end up as separated gas-phase atoms or radicals. Because breaking a bond always requires putting energy in to pull the attracted atoms apart, bond enthalpies are always reported as positive numbers, representing an endothermic process. The flip side is just as important: forming that same bond releases exactly that much energy, so bond formation is exothermic by the same magnitude. This sign convention, energy in to break, energy out to form, is the seed of the calculation method covered in the next chapter.

The word "average" in the definition matters. A specific C-H bond in a specific molecule, say the third C-H bond broken from a methane molecule that has already lost two hydrogens, does not take exactly the same energy to break as a C-H bond in ethanol or in benzene, because the rest of the molecule influences how tightly that particular bond is held. Chemists get around this by measuring the same type of bond across many different molecules and averaging the results, producing a single tabulated bond enthalpy for "C-H" or "O-H" or "C=O" that is a useful approximation rather than an exact value for any one specific molecule. This is also why bond enthalpy calculations, which you will use to estimate reaction enthalpies, give good estimates rather than exact matches to experimentally measured delta H values.

As a first worked example, consider the complete atomization of methane, breaking every bond in one mole of gas-phase CH4 so that only separated gas-phase atoms remain: CH4(g) -> C(g) + 4 H(g). Since methane has four equivalent C-H bonds, and the average C-H bond enthalpy is commonly tabulated as about 413 kJ/mol, the estimated energy required is 4 x 413 kJ/mol = 1652 kJ per mole of methane. This is a large amount of energy, which makes sense: you are not just loosening methane's structure, you are tearing every one of its four bonds completely apart into free atoms. If you compare this estimate to careful experimental measurements of the individual C-H bond dissociation energies in methane, the first bond broken actually takes somewhat more energy than the last one, since the molecular environment changes as each hydrogen is removed. The individual dissociation energies differ from each other and from the flat average of 413 kJ/mol, even though their sum is close to the 1652 kJ estimate. That is precisely the tradeoff bond enthalpy tables make: convenience and broad applicability in exchange for being an average rather than an exact value.

This connects directly back to enthalpy change as covered earlier: bond enthalpies are simply enthalpy changes for a very specific, standardized kind of process, gas-phase bond breaking, and like any enthalpy change they can be added and subtracted using the same Hess's law logic you have already practiced. That is exactly the tool built in the next chapter, where bond enthalpies for reactants and products are combined to estimate the enthalpy of an entire reaction.
